extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, and copyeditors using the Chicago Manual of Style guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for formatting numbers, inclusive ranges, telephone numbers, and abbreviations (acronyms, initialisms, contractions, titles, degrees, place names, and addresses) according to the Chicago Manual of Style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing in digit groups and decimal marker
rubrics_metrics.description: No space is used for groups of only four digits either to the left or to the right of the decimal marker (except in table columns that also include numbers having five or more digits, where it is needed for alignment). To mark the decimal, either a decimal point or a comma may be used, according to what is customary in a given context or region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 3 426 869 0.000 007 2501.4865 (or 2 501.486 5). See also rules 6.121, 9.54-55 for further SI-unit and decimal guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone number formatting (U.S./Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: US/Canada telephone numbers conventionally include prefix 1 (trunk prefix), an area code, and a seven-digit number (three-digit exchange + four-digit line). When written, the seven-digit number is conventionally separated by a hyphen; area code is often placed in parentheses to show optionality for local calls; prefix 1 can usually be omitted. An extension follows the number, separated by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable forms: (000) 000-0000 or (1-000) 000-0000; (000) 000-0000, ext. 0000. An alternative style drops parentheses for area code (000-000-0000 or 1-000-000-0000). Be consistent. Periods or other punctuation as separators in place of hyphens are generally not recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: International telephone numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: For international numbers, use spaces rather than hyphens as separators. A plus symbol stands in for the international prefix and is placed immediately before the country code with no intervening space. Parentheses should not be used for international numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: +52 55 0000 0000; +66 2000 0000; +44 20 0000 0000. If an international prefix must be expressed, it precedes the country code and is separated by a space (e.g., 011 44 20 ...). For a US/Canadian number written for an international audience, include country code (e.g., +1 607 000 0000). Consult ITU standards or local directories for country-specific conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratios: text and numeral forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratios composed of whole numbers may generally be expressed using 'to' and spelled out in ordinary text; where numerals are preferred, use a colon as a shorthand for 'to' with no spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a three-to-one ratio' or 'a 13-to-2 ratio' or 'a 13:2 ratio'. In some contexts ratios may be expressed as decimal fractions similar to percentages (see percentages guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inclusive en dash for ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: An en dash used between two numbers implies up to and including, or through (inclusive range).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Please refer to pages 75–110.' 'Here are the figures for 2000–2009.' 'Campers were divided into age groups 5–7, 8–10...' Do not use an en dash if 'from' or 'between' is used before the first number; use 'from...to' or 'between...and' instead (e.g., 'from 75 to 110', not 'from 75–110'). Inclusive spelled-out numbers should be joined by 'to' (e.g., 'participants aged forty-five to forty-nine years'). See 6.78–84 for en dash usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating (condensing) inclusive numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago's system for abbreviated inclusive numbers prescribes which digits to repeat and which to shorten in the second number of a range to be efficient and unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules and examples: Less than 100 — use all digits: 3–10, 71–72, 96–117. 100 or multiples of 100 — use all digits: 100–104, 1100–1113. 101–109 — use changed part only: 101–8. 201–209 etc. — 808–33. 110–199, 210–299 etc. — use two digits unless more are needed: 321–28, 498–532, 1087–89. When change extends into thousands or beyond, repeat all digits to avoid ambiguity: 6,000–6,018; 12,473–79; 1,247,689–710; 1,247,689–1,248,125. Inclusive years may be abbreviated similarly, but when the century changes or in BCE/BC/BP sequences, include all digits: 1897–1901; 1914–18; fiscal year 2017–18 or 2017/18; 2000–2001. In book titles respect original form. For exceptions, full-form everywhere is foolproof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman numerals: formation and preferred use
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman numerals are formed by additive and subtractive combinations of letters (I, V, X, L, C, D, M); a bar multiplies value by 1,000. Chicago prefers arabic numerals in many contexts where roman numerals were formerly common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: table of common roman ↔ arabic values provided. Note historical variants (e.g., IIII on clock faces) and that inclusive roman numerals are always given in full. Exceptions where roman numerals are used are treated elsewhere (front matter, legal instruments, names of monarchs, outline style, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: acronym, initialism, contraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronym: initials read as a word (AIDS, laser, NASA, scuba). Initialism: initials read as a series of letters (IRS, NBA, XML). Contraction: abbreviations that include the first and last letters of the full word (Mr., amt.). The chapter uses 'abbreviation' as umbrella term for these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note imperfect boundaries (XML's X = initial sound; FAQ can be pronounced as word or letters). Symbols (©) sometimes abbreviate terms; abbreviations for units may be called symbols in SI usage. For technical abbreviations consult subject-specific manuals (e.g., Scientific Style and Format).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use abbreviations generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside science and technology, abbreviations and symbols are most appropriate in tabular matter, notes, bibliographies, and parenthetical references; some expressions are commonly abbreviated in regular prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like ATM, DNA, Ms., NASA may be used without spelling out; less familiar abbreviations should be spelled out at first occurrence and limited to terms that occur roughly five times or more within an article or chapter. The abbreviation usually follows immediately in parentheses but may be introduced in other ways. Do not introduce an abbreviation that will be used only once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing many abbreviations in a document
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and editors should monitor the number of different abbreviations used; provide a list of abbreviations in works with many unfamiliar terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an abbreviation reappears after a long interval, consider repeating the spelled-out form as a reminder. For plural forms of abbreviations and 'a/an/the' with abbreviations see other rules (7.15, 7.33, 10.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods with abbreviations (general rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago recommends general guidelines for using periods with abbreviations in nontechnical settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 1: Use periods with abbreviations that end in a lowercase letter: p. (page), vol., e.g., i.e., etc., a.k.a., a.m., p.m., Ms., Dr., et al. (et is not an abbreviation; al. is). Exception for some academic degrees. Rule 2: Use periods for initials standing for given names: E. B. White; do not use periods for an entire name replaced by initials: JFK. Rule 3: Use no periods with abbreviations that include two or more capital letters, even if the abbreviation also includes lowercase letters: VP, CEO, MA, MD, PhD, UK, US, NY, IL (see rule 4). Rule 4: In publications using traditional state abbreviations, use periods to abbreviate United States and its states and territories: U.S., N.Y., Ill.; Chicago prefers the two-letter postal codes (US) wherever abbreviations are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and spacing between elements
rubrics_metrics.description: No space is left between the letters of initialisms and acronyms. Space is usually left between abbreviated words, unless an abbreviated word is used in combination with a single-letter abbreviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: RN Gov. Gen. but C-SPAN Mng. Ed. S. Dak. (see 10.27 for state forms). Follow personal-name rules at 10.12. For units of measure in scientific usage, periods are generally omitted (see 10.49–68).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of acronyms and initialisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Initialisms tend to appear in all capital letters. With frequent use, acronyms (especially longer ones) may become lowercase words (scuba); acronyms derived from proper nouns will retain an initial capital (Unicef). Chicago generally prefers all-capital form unless Webster's lists otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect scientific conventions (e.g., mRNA, IgG, bp) where such forms are standard. Examples: NAFTA (not Nafta).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of words in spelled-out expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in a spelled-out version of an acronym or initialism are capitalized only if they are proper nouns; otherwise they should generally be lowercased, even when appearing alongside abbreviated form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) — words capitalized as proper nouns; transmission-control protocol/internet protocol (TCP/IP) — lowercased when not proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics vs roman for abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize an abbreviation only if the spelled-out term would be italicized (titles of books, periodicals, etc.); common Latin abbreviations are set in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: OED (Oxford English Dictionary) — no italics for abbreviation; JAMA (Journal of the American Medical Association). Latin abbrevs like ibid., etc., e.g., i.e. are roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small capitals vs full-size capitals for acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some designs call for small capitals, but Chicago does not generally recommend small capitals; if used, the editor should decide and apply them on the final manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit small capitals to acronyms/initialisms in running text; avoid applying to two-letter postal codes in notes or bibliographies or to roman numerals. Check after conversion to publication that small caps haven't reverted to lowercase or full capitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of 'a' or 'an' before abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abbreviation follows an indefinite article, the choice of 'a' or 'an' is determined by how the abbreviation would be read aloud (its pronunciation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acronyms read as words are rarely preceded by a/an/the unless adjectival. Examples: an HMO (pronounced 'aitch em oh'); a UFO (a yoo-eff-oh); a NATO member (NATO read as a word). See 10.2 and 7.33.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite article with initialisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Initialisms read as letters are often preceded by a definite article when the spelled-out form would be (e.g., 'the NBA'), but practice depends on established usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no established usage, use the definite article if it would be used with the spelled-out form. Some terms (e.g., DIY) do not ordinarily require a definite article in spelled-out form and therefore not as an initialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampersand usage inside abbreviations/initialisms
rubrics_metrics.description: No space is left on either side of an ampersand used within an initialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R&D; Texas A&M. See also company-name guidance in 14.135.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for personal given names and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally, abbreviations should not be used for given names; a signature should be transcribed as the person wrote it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of historical abbreviations: Benj. Franklin; Geo. D. Fuller. For transcription of signatures follow original form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initials in personal names: periods and spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Initials standing for given names are followed by a period and a space. A period is normally used even if the middle initial does not stand for a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roger W. Shugg; P. D. James; M. F. K. Fisher. Do not use periods for a whole name replaced by initials (JFK).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire-name abbreviations (initialisms) formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: If an entire name is abbreviated, spaces and periods can usually be omitted (initialism form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FDR (Franklin Delano Roosevelt), MJ (Michael Jordan), JLo (Jennifer Lopez) — note style variants like J.Lo (album title) where punctuation is part of the stylized form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating titles before names
rubrics_metrics.description: Many civil or military titles preceding a full name may be abbreviated. When preceding a surname alone, titles should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rep. Dan Lipinski; Representative Lipinski. Sen. Kirsten E. Gillibrand; Senator Gillibrand. If space is tight, certain abbreviations (Rep., Sen., Gov., Pres., etc.) may precede a full name, but use full form before surname alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil-title abbreviation usage and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A selective list of civil-title abbreviations may be used before a full name where space is tight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: Ald., Atty. Gen., Insp. Gen., Prof., Assoc. Prof., Fr., Judge, Adv. Gen., Sr. Use spelled-out form when preceding a surname alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military rank abbreviations and branch variants
rubrics_metrics.description: US military official abbreviated ranks omit periods; abbreviations for ranks may vary across branches; traditional abbreviations are preferred in general contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Adm. vs ADM variants; SSG vs S.Sgt. Branch differences exist (army, air force, marines). For the latest official forms consult US Department of Defense websites; for Canadian/UK forces consult their respective official sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social titles abbreviation and omission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Social titles (Ms., Mr., Mrs., Mx., Dr.) are always abbreviated whether preceding the full name or the surname only. Social titles are routinely omitted in most prose; academic degrees or professional designations following a name make preceding titles unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jennifer James, MD (not Dr. Jennifer James, MD). The archaic Esq. is used only after a full name and never when Mr., Dr., etc. precede the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: French social titles punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: For French social titles used untranslated in English settings, Mme and Mlle are considered contractions and therefore do not take a period; observe French usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms: M., MM., Mme, Mlle. When Monsieur/Madame used without a name in direct address, spell out (and in French usually lowercase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for 'Reverend' and 'Honorable'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rev. and Hon. are traditionally used before a full name when 'the' does not precede the title. With 'the', spell out the title. With a last name only such titles are normally omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rev. Sam Portaro; the Reverend Sam Portaro. Hon. Henry M. Brown; the Honorable Henry M. Brown. Use 'Reverend So-and-So' in informal prose or speech where common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffixes like Jr., Sr., III as part of a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations for 'Junior', 'Senior', and numeric suffixes (Jr., Sr., III, 3rd) are part of the name and are retained with any titles or honorifics. These abbreviations are used only with the full name, never with the surname alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jordan Balfence Jr. spoke first. In some contexts (e.g., biographies) it may be appropriate to use Jr. or Sr. with a first name alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating names of saints
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'Saint' is often abbreviated (St., pl. Sts.) before the name of a Christian saint; it should normally be spelled out in formal prose but may be abbreviated where space is at a premium. Choose consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Saint (or St.) Teresa. When 'Saint' or 'St.' forms part of a personal name, follow the bearer's usage (e.g., Augustus Saint-Gaudens; Muriel St. Clare Byrne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic degrees: punctuation and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago recommends omitting periods in abbreviations of academic degrees (BA, DDS, etc.) unless required by tradition or consistency. Spelled-out degree names should be lowercased in normal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of common degree abbreviations provided (AB, AM, BA, BFA, BS, PhD, JD, MD, etc.). When following a personal name, these designations are set off by commas: Ariel Z. Lee, JD, attended law school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional, religious, and other designations formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations for many professional and other designations follow the academic-degree pattern; Chicago recommends dispensing with periods. Spelled-out terms are lowercase unless they are proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: RN, CNM, FAIA, FRS, MP, OFM, RN set off by commas when following a name: Joan Hotimlanska, LPN, will be working on the second floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common abbreviations for companies and firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations like Assoc., Inc., Bros., Co., Corp., Ltd., Mfg., PLC may be used; use periods or not according to general punctuation rules (see 10.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In running text company names are best given in full, but many full forms include ampersands and abbreviations. If in doubt, look up the company name in authoritative sources. Elements like Inc., & Co., LLC may be omitted unless relevant to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media company call letters formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast call letters (ABC, CBS, HBO, MTV, NBC, etc.) are always capitalized and do not take periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use without periods in running text and lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations and agencies initialisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of agencies and organizations commonly abbreviated as initialisms appear in full capitals and without periods in running text and tabular matter (preferably after being spelled out on first occurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AAUP, EU, WHO, AFL-CIO, HMO (pl. HMOs), WTO, EPA. For 'a/an/the' with abbreviations see rule 10.9.

rubrics_metrics.name: US states and territories abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: In running text, spell out names of states, territories, and possessions when standing alone and preferably when following a city; in bibliographies, tables, mailing addresses, and lists they are usually abbreviated. Chicago prefers two-letter postal codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal codes (AK, AL, AR, CA, etc.) are preferred; traditional abbreviations (Calif., Ill., etc.) may be used where required but Chicago recommends the two-letter postal codes where abbreviations are used. See 6.39, 6.17 for comma rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canadian provinces and territories abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Canadian provinces and territories are normally spelled out in running text but may be abbreviated in bibliographies and the like — use two-letter postal abbreviations which work for both English and French forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AB (Alberta), BC (British Columbia), MB (Manitoba), ON (Ontario), QC (Quebec/Québec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with city plus state abbreviation
rubrics_metrics.description: When following the name of a city, the names of states, provinces, and territories are enclosed in commas whether spelled out (running text) or abbreviated (lists/tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bedford, PA, and Jamestown, NY. Exception: no comma between the postal code and a zip code in addresses (Send to Quartz, IL 60000).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating place-name generic elements (Fort, Mount, Saint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic terms in geographic names are usually spelled out in formal prose but can be abbreviated where space is at a premium or to reflect predominant usage. 'San' and 'Santa' are never abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fort (Ft.) Myers; Mount (Mt.) Airy; Port (Pt.) Arthur; Saint (St.) Paul; Saint (St.) Louis. Use consistent style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating country names and codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Country names are usually spelled out in running text but may be abbreviated in tables and the like; use discretion and define abbreviations in table notes if there is risk of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of short forms: Fr., Ger., Isr., It., Neth., Russ., Sp. Use established initialisms after the full form has been given (UAE, US, UK). For technical uses consider ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 or alpha-3 codes where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'US' vs 'United States'
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago historically advised spelling out 'United States' as a noun and reserving 'US' for adjective use, but now permits the use of 'US' as a noun subject to editorial discretion and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'US dollars' or 'United States involvement in China' — use editorial judgment and consistency across a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailing-address abbreviations: postal vs standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Postal-service standard abbreviations for mailing addresses are all caps and do not use periods and are most appropriate for mailing addresses. In tabular matter Chicago prefers the standard abbreviated forms (with conventional capitalization). In running text spell out instead of abbreviating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AVE / Ave.; BLDG / Bldg.; RD / Rd.; ST / St.; STE / Ste. For postal forms consult USPS or regional postal services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compass-point abbreviations in mailing addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-letter compass points accompanying a street name are normally followed by a period; two-letter compass points are not. The USPS does not use periods for either; when used in an address, NE, NW, SE, SW remain abbreviated even in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1060 E. Prospect Ave. (or in running text 1060 East Prospect Avenue); 456 NW Lane St. (or in running text 456 NW Lane Street); 'N Street SW' — here 'N' is a street name, not a compass point. Do not abbreviate compass points that are part of a street/place name (South Ave., Northwest Hwy.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for compass points and technical usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of the compass may be abbreviated without periods: N, E, S, W, NE, SE, SW, NW, NNE, ENE, ESE, etc.; variants like 'N by NE' are also used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal nontechnical text these terms are usually spelled out; use abbreviations primarily in technical contexts, tables, or addresses.
